content: UNITAID is an international organization established to facilitate the procurement of medications targeting HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis. It was founded in September 2006 through the collaborative efforts of Brazil and France. A significant portion of its funding is derived from innovative development financing mechanisms, such as a solidarity levy imposed on airline tickets. By April 2007, UNITAID had 35 member states, and its budget was projected to exceed $500 million by 2009, with at least 85% of these funds allocated to low-income countries. The organization operates under the auspices of the World Health Organization (WHO) in Geneva. Its primary strength lies in leveraging its substantial financial resources to negotiate reduced drug prices. However, UNITAID does not directly manage medication distribution programs; instead, it supports initiatives led by partner organizations, including The Global Fund, the Clinton Foundation, and the WHO. The establishment of UNITAID was preceded by two pivotal reports on innovative financing mechanisms. The first, the Report of the Technical Group on Innovative Financing Mechanisms, was commissioned by the heads of state of Brazil, Chile, France, and Spain and published in September 2004. The second, the Landau Report, was requested by French President Jacques Chirac and released in December 2004. Both documents explored various innovative financing opportunities, emphasizing the stability and predictability of tax-based models. Following these publications, the involved countries sought to draw international attention to innovative development financing. For example, in February 2005, Brazil, Chile, France, Germany, and Spain issued a joint statement proposing ideas for financing the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). Later that year, during a UN meeting in New York, a declaration was made advocating for further exploration of innovative financing sources. This was followed by an international conference titled Solidarity and Globalization: Innovative Financing for Development and Against Pandemics, held in Paris from February 28 to March 1, 2006. Subsequently, a pilot group of 44 countries was formed to explore innovative financing, and France introduced a solidarity tax on airline tickets, which took effect on July 1, 2006. Finally, on September 17, 2006, UNITAID was officially founded by Brazil, Chile, France, Norway, and the United Kingdom, although not all of these countries utilized airline ticket taxation to fulfill their commitments. Since its inception, additional countries, including 18 African nations, have joined the initiative, contributing to UNITAID's funding as of February 2007. UNITAID's primary mission is to ensure access to medications for combating the world's most lethal diseases—HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis. Its secondary objectives include negotiating lower prices for existing medications through bulk purchasing and promoting the development and mass production of specialized drugs that are either unavailable or unaffordable. Examples include pediatric formulations for HIV/AIDS-infected children and second-line drugs for individuals resistant to standard treatments. Notable achievements include a 40% price reduction in antiretroviral therapy for 100,000 children with AIDS across 34 Asian and African countries by the end of 2007, in partnership with the Clinton Foundation. Additionally, UNITAID has funded tuberculosis treatment for 150,000 children since September 2007, in collaboration with the Stop TB Partnership and the Global Drug Facility. It has also supported the provision of artemisinin-based combination therapies for malaria in 19 countries, working with UNICEF and The Global Fund. Furthermore, UNITAID finances a WHO program for drug prequalification and assists UNICEF in supplying HIV test kits and antiretroviral treatments to pregnant women. UNITAID's organizational structure is streamlined due to its focused scope of activities. The President serves as the official representative of the organization. On March 3, 2007, French Foreign Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy was elected as UNITAID's President for a two-year term. The Secretariat, based in Geneva within WHO facilities, manages the organization's daily operations. On May 4, 2007, Dr. Jorge Antonio Zepeda Bermudez of Brazil assumed the role of UNITAID's Executive Secretary. The Board, which is the decision-making body, determines how funds are allocated, establishes partnerships, sets future objectives, and formulates action plans. The Board comprises ten members, including representatives from the founding countries (Brazil, Chile, France, Norway, and the United Kingdom), one representative from Africa (selected by the African Union), one from Asia (South Korea), two from civil society (NGOs and communities affected by the diseases), and one from the WHO.
